- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.20) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or shift downward.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >85.00), model often overshoots and fails to correct; apply a “cool-down” bias to dampen upward momentum.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 80.00), model overreacts; adjust forecast to align with recent mean.
- In sentiment-heavy periods (e.g., 0.20–0.40), model often underestimates volatility; increase forecast variance or add upward bias for high-sentiment windows.
- For 30-day horizon, model frequently overpredicts early in the window; apply a “lag correction” to reduce initial forecast values.
- When true outcome shows strong upward trend after low sentiment, model underestimates; adjust forecast to reflect sentiment shift.
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.00 values, model tends to be overly conservative; increase forecast slightly to avoid underestimation.
- In high-sentiment windows (≥0.20), model often fails to capture sentiment-driven spikes; add a sentiment multiplier to forecast (e.g., +0.10 to +0.30) if sentiment >0.20.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows a sharp drop after a spike, model often fails to anticipate; apply a “reversal buffer” to reduce forecast slope after high peaks.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome by >5.00, apply a “floor correction” to cap forecast at 5–10% below recent high.
